summary: Daily sales team meeting run by Chris Klevan with closers Harry Edmonds, Ben Byrne and Andrew Musial, and setter Kyla Louie. Ben Byrne introduces himself as a new hire — his first fitness offer. The team shares wins, then discusses dialler tactics for getting prospects to pick up, including what caller name to display and what name setters give. Roughly 25 minutes are given over to Chris and Ben coaching Harry through a personal crisis about detachment, money and whether closing people is the right thing to do. The meeting then runs projections: Harry at one unit and $3,000 for the week, Andrew projected two units with no closes yet, Kyla at five sets with three calls booked for the day. It closes with a review of Andrew's lost Jorge Fernández call from the previous day, in which Ben and Chris both conclude the prospect had no burning reason to buy.
notable: Caller identity. Chris Klevan describes his own dialler practice: 'I like to just tell them, I usually just write, like, say, Trevor Instinct, and then usually people just answer because they think it's Trevor.' Kyla Louie describes using a false first name from a Matt Ryder video — 'he just says, hey, this is Jess... I've tried it. It works' — and Chris endorses it: 'That's cool. It's not a bad idea. I like it.' Harry calls it 'textbook Matt Ryder psycho'. Kyla adds she has 'been figuring out some fun methods to get through the Google Voice'.
Setter roster confirmed: 'Every time Kyla and Kim put a set on your calendar' — Kyla Louie is the KL suffix in call titles and Kim is the other setter, mapping to KFS.

A closer raised a live conscience objection to closing. Harry Edmonds: 'I think that sometimes it could be a lack of conviction in, is the right thing to do to close them... I know that I have the skill to sit there and battle with this person and close them, but I think that sometimes that doesn't feel like the right thing to do.' Chris Klevan's response: 'But is that your decision to make? Is it your decision to decide whether or not somebody deserves to be closed or not?' Ben Byrne: 'So what would a situation be where someone would be on a call for an hour, but it wouldn't be the right thing to close them?'

Prospect reluctance was framed as something to be overcome rather than heard. Chris on a prospect saying no: 'Are they flat out telling you they don't want to do it, or is it just programming?' and, on the Jorge call, 'help move him up to a point to where he can start to want to actually make the change, feel angry enough about his situation, like challenge him a little bit to actually rise him up.'

Harry described marathon objection handling approvingly: 'I've sat on three and a half hour sales calls just to objection handle for two hours and close them. I've got one recorded somewhere... You gave me 57 objections and I closed it.'

Show rate is not being tracked. Chris: 'Where are we at show rate-wise right now?' Kyla: 'I'm not sure on the exact percentage.' Chris: 'Is there a way for me to check?' He asks her to bring it from the Piff Perfect dashboard in future.

Weekly numbers as stated: Harry at 'one unit so far on Monday' recorded as $3,000, which does not match either the $6,000 or $9,000 list price and is consistent with a first instalment being reported rather than contract value. Andrew Musial projected at two units with no close yet — 'Are we going to see our first deal hit the line today?'

The company already runs an AI sales-call analyser and distrusts its scores. Chris: 'that AI analyzer is the reason I review every single call still manually, because it's just not to be completely trusted.' Relevant context for how any automated scoring of this corpus will be received.

Post-mortem on the Jorge Fernández call was substantively correct. Ben Byrne: 'now we're talking about giving $6,000 to a stranger on the internet to prove it to himself? Is there a big enough burning problem for him to actually change?' Chris: 'Definitely not.' Andrew self-identified the failure as misalignment and a missed longevity hook.

Harry Edmonds disclosed a great deal of personal material in a recorded group setting — that he is 22, lives at his mother's house, does not feel empathy, and would not shed a tear at his grandmother's death — under sustained questioning from two managers.
